365.title: The conquerors
365.hook: emperors who conquered every land, with drums beating, also went without the Name (Savaiye)
365.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this among the Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning, and the nagara, the great kettledrum, is still beaten at some gurdwaras and in Sikh processions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maate matang, maddened elephants, and your line, they left empty-handed. Today, a verse you can hear before you see it.

Before you see an army in the old world, you hear it. A low thudding comes over the hills, then another and another, until the ground itself seems to beat. Kettledrums, war drums, the big nagaras, carried in front of the march so every village knows who's coming. Kings had them beaten when they set out and again when they came home with a new country in their pocket. Now listen for the moment after the march has passed, when the last beat rolls away down the valley.
screen: `A THUDDING OVER THE HILLS.` → `NAGARAS IN FRONT OF THE MARCH.` → `THE LAST BEAT ROLLS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Among the ten savaiye is a verse made of that sound. In paraphrase: they went out and conquered every land in every direction, with drums and kettledrums beating. Their elephants trumpeted, their horses neighed by the thousand. Kings like these, past, present and to come, can't be counted. Then the turn the savaiye keep making: without remembering the Lord, at the end they all went to their final home. Beside it stands another savaiya, about warriors in shining armor so sure of themselves they thought even mountains couldn't move them. They too go. The striking thing is the man writing it. Guru Gobind Singh had a great drum of his own. Sikh tradition remembers the Ranjit Nagara, a huge kettledrum made at Anandpur, beaten morning and evening, whose boom worried the hill kings around him. Sikhs still beat a nagara at some gurdwaras and in processions today. So this isn't someone who hated drums; he knew how good it felt to hear your own. The verse's point is simpler and harder. The sound of victory is real, and it fades. The conquerors are measured not by how far their drums carried, but by whether they remembered the One who outlasts every march. In the Sikh view, that remembering, simran, is what keeps sounding after the last beat. So the verse is said in the quiet of early morning, before the day's own drums start up: deadlines, targets, scoreboards. They're allowed to beat. The verse just counts how long each one lasts.
screen: `THEY CONQUERED EVERY LAND.` · `WITHOUT THE NAME, THEY STILL WENT.` · `THE GURU'S OWN GREAT DRUM.` · `VICTORY IS REAL, AND IT FADES.` · then, large: `DRUMS FADE.`

segments.voice: Listen for a minute to the sounds around you, near and far, and notice how each one rises and fades. Then find one small thing you've been pushing for mostly to be seen winning, more likes, the last word, being first, and hold it lightly, like a drumbeat already rolling away. You don't have to give up every goal; if you pray, say Waheguru as you set this one down.
The conquerors. A savaiya of kettledrums and conquered lands: kings beyond counting, who at the end still went without the Name.
Your line: drums fade. Remembering keeps sounding. Three hundred sixty-five days: a whole year of days, walked.

screen: `DAY 365 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EYES SHUT LIKE A CRANE.`

366.title: Eyes shut like a crane
366.hook: what is gained by closing both eyes and sitting like a crane, pretending (Savaiye)
366.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya each morning as part of the Tav Prasad Savaiye, and practice simran, quiet repetition of the Name, often with eyes closed and away from any audience.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the conquerors, and your line, drums fade. Today, a bird that looks very holy.

Watch a heron or a crane at the edge of a pond. It stands perfectly still on one leg, head drawn in, eyes half closed. Minutes go by. If you didn't know better, you'd say it was deep in meditation, the calmest creature in the field. Then a fish flickers past its feet, and in a flash the beak is in the water and the fish is gone. The stillness was never peace. It was patience with an appetite. That bird became a byword long ago.
screen: `A CRANE ON ONE LEG, EYES HALF SHUT.` → `IT LOOKS LIKE MEDITATION.` → `THEN THE FISH IS GONE.`

segments.voice: In Punjabi and the languages around it, there's an old name for a show-off saint: a crane devotee, someone who looks holy while watching for the fish. Guru Gobind Singh uses that very bird in one of the savaiye. In paraphrase: what is gained by shutting both eyes and sitting like a crane in meditation? He bathed in the seven seas, and lost this world and the next. He spent his life among the things he craved, and so the days went by. The phrase is bak dhiaan, crane meditation. It doesn't laugh at stillness. Sikhs sit in stillness too, in simran, repeating the Name, often with eyes closed. The target isn't the closed eyes. It's what's going on behind them: the crane's eyes are shut, but its mind is on the fish. So the question turns on anyone who prays. When your eyes are closed, what are you watching for? Being seen as devout? Getting something? Or the One you say you're turning toward? The Guru Granth Sahib uses the same bird, the white crane that looks spotless and is still hunting, so the image runs deep in Sikh teaching. And this verse ends on a line we'll stay with on day three hundred sixty-eight, the one the whole set leans toward. For today: stillness for show is just a crane at a pond. The verse asks for the other kind, the kind nobody sees.
screen: `THE CRANE: STILL, BUT HUNTING.` · `WHAT IS GAINED BY SHUTTING YOUR EYES?` · `NOT THE EYES, BUT WHAT'S BEHIND THEM.` · `STILLNESS NOBODY SEES.` · then, large: `NOT FOR SHOW.`

segments.voice: Find a spot where nobody can see you, not even a camera, and pray, or simply sit, with no one watching. Notice if some part of you is still performing, sitting a bit straighter, imagining how this looks, and let it go. If you pray, say Waheguru once, quietly, for the One it's for; if not, be still for its own sake.
Bak dhiaan, crane meditation. Stillness that looks holy while the mind waits for the fish.
Your line: not for show. What counts is what's behind the eyes. Until tomorrow, then.

367.title: Every outward ritual
367.hook: the Tenth Guru lists outward practices of many kinds and says all miss the secret without love (Savaiye)
367.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite these verses as part of the Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning, and gurdwara teachers often apply them to Sikh practice itself, warning against rituals done without love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bak dhiaan, crane meditation, and your line, not for show. Today the savaiye widen the circle.

Make a list of everything people in one town do to be religious. Some wear something around their neck. Some keep a special object in the house. Some face a certain direction to pray. Some walk to a holy place, some fast, some give to charity, some read the same book every day for years. A poet looks at all of it at once, his own neighbors and his own people too, and asks one quiet question of every practice. Not is it right, or whose is best. Just: is the secret inside it?
screen: `WHAT PEOPLE DO TO BE RELIGIOUS.` → `ALL AT ONCE, NEIGHBORS AND OWN.` → `IS THE SECRET INSIDE IT?`

segments.voice: Two of the savaiye make long lists like this. One, in paraphrase: bathing at pilgrim places, compassion, restraint, charity, vows and disciplines of many kinds; reading the scriptures of many peoples; living on air, keeping celibacy, weighing a thousand opinions. Without the Lord, not one of these counts for anything. The other lists the outward signs of the Guru's world, things people carried, wore, faced and bowed to, the practices of the communities all around him. It ends: the whole world is tangled in false, outward rites, and no one has found the secret of the Lord. The word for secret is bhed, the hidden thing, what's actually going on inside. Hear it fairly. The verse names practices of the Guru's neighbors, but it isn't a list of other people's mistakes. Compassion and charity are on it, things the Sikh Gurus taught constantly, so it can't mean they're bad. It means they're empty when done for their own sake, as a box to tick. Sikh teachers are quick to turn it on Sikh habits too: bowing to the Guru Granth Sahib without listening to it, keeping the outward form while the heart is elsewhere, saying the Nitnem fast to get it done. The secret, the savaiye have been saying all week, is love. A ritual with love in it is alive. The same ritual without it is a costume.
screen: `TWO LISTS OF EVERY PRACTICE.` · `NO ONE FOUND THE SECRET, THE BHED.` · `COMPASSION IS ON THE LIST TOO.` · `TURNED ON SIKH HABITS AS WELL.` · then, large: `THE SECRET IS LOVE.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you do regularly, religious or not, a prayer, a visit, a call to a parent, a family dinner, and walk through it in your mind. Ask gently: is there love in it right now, or has it become a box I tick? Don't judge the answer, just see it clearly, and if you pray, let Waheguru sit with it.
Bhed, the hidden thing. The savaiye's long lists of practices, and the line that says the whole world is tangled in them and hasn't found the secret.
Your line: the secret is love. The heart, not the count. Day three hundred sixty-seven, done.

screen: `DAY 367 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND HIM.`

368.title: Those who loved found Him
368.hook: I tell the truth, listen all: those who loved found the Lord (Savaiye)
368.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya each morning as part of the Tav Prasad Savaiye, and its closing line is widely quoted and sung in kirtan as a summary of the Sikh teaching on love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhed, the hidden thing, and your line, the secret is love. Today, the line the savaiye have been leaning toward.

A family dinner, a meeting, a wedding speech that's gone on a bit. People are half-listening, checking phones. Then someone stands and says: I'm going to tell you the truth now. Everyone listen. The room goes quiet, because that's not a sentence you say lightly. It means everything up to now was warm-up. One of the savaiye has exactly that sentence in it, after all the elephants and conquerors and cranes.
screen: `I'M GOING TO TELL YOU THE TRUTH.` → `EVERYONE LISTEN.` → `THE ROOM GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: Here it is, transliterated: saach kahoon sun leho sabhai, jin prem kio tin hee prabh paaio. Saach kahoon: I speak the truth. Sun leho sabhai: listen, all of you. Jin prem kio: those who loved. Tin hee prabh paaio: they alone found the Lord. Two small details make this line. First, hee, that little word. Not those who loved also found Him, among others. Only they. After all the parades, the ascetics and the drums and the rituals, one road is left standing. Second, the tense. Found. The verse doesn't speak like a theory about how someone might reach God. It speaks like a witness reporting what has already happened. What kind of love? Sikhs hear it as prem, a whole-hearted longing for the One that changes how you live. Guru Nanak has a saying in the Guru Granth Sahib that helps. In paraphrase: if you want to play this game of love, come to my lane with your head in your hand. So it isn't a soft feeling. It costs. Sikh tradition remembers many who loved that way, all the way. But the Gurus also show that love starts small: in seva, in langar, in how you treat the person in front of you. You can't love God, Sikhs often say, and be careless with the people God made. It fits that the line closes the crane verse. You can fake stillness. You can fake ritual. Love is the one thing that doesn't work as a performance.

segments.voice: Let a face come to mind, someone you love but haven't told lately: a parent, a sibling, a friend, a partner. Picture them clearly and find one specific thing you love about them. If you pray, hold them in Waheguru; if not, simply hold them in your attention for a while.
Prem, whole-hearted love. Jin prem kio tin hee prabh paaio: those who loved, they alone found the Lord. The line the savaiye lean toward.
Your line: those who loved, found. Love that costs, and starts small. See you tomorrow, friend.

369.title: Savaiye close
369.hook: the ten verses sharpen one point: love, not display
369.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite all ten Tav Prasad Savaiye each morning after Jaap Sahib; they are also read while amrit is prepared at the Khalsa initiation, where initiates take on the five articles of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, prem, the line at the heart of the savaiye, and yours: those who loved, found. Today we close the ten verses.

Here's a strange thing about the man who wrote the ten savaiye. Guru Gobind Singh gave the Khalsa its outward form: the five articles Sikhs who take amrit keep on their bodies every day, uncut hair, a comb, a steel bracelet, cotton undershorts, the kirpan. He shaped how a whole community looks, to this day. And the same Guru wrote ten verses saying outward forms, without love, aren't worth a single seed. Is that a contradiction?
screen: `THE GURU WHO GAVE THE KHALSA ITS FORM.` → `WROTE THAT FORM WITHOUT LOVE IS NOTHING.` → `A CONTRADICTION?`

segments.voice: First, lay the ten verses side by side. They make the same move every time: set up something impressive, then weigh it. Tav prasad over the door: cupped hands, waiting. The ascetics of every order: not one ratti without love. Maate matang: their kings left barefoot. The conquerors: the drums faded. The crane with its eyes shut: still, and hunting. Bhed, with compassion and charity on the list: the secret missed. Then the line the set leans on: those who loved, they alone found the Lord. Ten verses, one point, sharpened until it cuts. Love, not display. Now the question from the hook. Sikhs don't hear the savaiye as saying the outward form doesn't matter. The same verses are recited while the amrit is prepared, at the very ceremony where people take on the five articles. So the form and the warning are given in the same breath, on purpose. As some Sikh teachers put it, the form is meant to carry the love, the way a cup carries water. A beautiful cup that's empty is still empty, but nobody throws it away for that. They fill it. The danger the savaiye name is the cup admired for itself: the turban worn for show, the bani rushed to be done, the kirpan as a costume. And the savaiye let no one off: not kings, not yogis, not pilgrims. Many readers hear the warning reaching the Khalsa too, since these verses are said at its own initiation.

370.title: A prayer for protection
370.hook: the Tenth Guru's quiet prayer asking to be sheltered
370.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Chaupai Sahib every morning as part of the Nitnem and again within the evening Rehras, and many also say it before travel, at night, or in times of fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ten savaiye closed, and your line was love, not display. Now a new bani begins, a quieter one.

Some prayers are made for a crowd, sung by a whole hall at once. Others are made for one person, very quietly: under your breath in the car on the way to the hospital, at three in the morning when the house makes a noise, on a plane as the wheels leave the ground. The Tenth Guru, who wrote war poetry and praise as wide as the sky, also wrote one of those. A small, close prayer, whose own heading calls it a request.
screen: `PRAYERS MADE FOR A CROWD.` → `AND PRAYERS UNDER YOUR BREATH.` → `THE TENTH GURU WROTE ONE.`

segments.voice: Benti means a humble request, the kind you make to someone greater than you, standing at their door. Chaupai is the meter: verses whose lines fall into four parts. Its heading in the Dasam Granth reads, roughly, the poet speaks: a request, in chaupai. It's short enough to learn by heart, which many Sikhs do. It's one of the five banis of the Sikh morning, it's in the evening Rehras, and it's recited while the amrit is prepared. One honest note: Sikhs don't all stop it in the same place. Some traditions recite a longer version, some a shorter one, with a few extra verses at the end. Both are said with devotion, and this path follows the common pattern without ranking either. The prayer opens with four lines, and its whole shape is in them. In paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. May my mind stay at your feet. Take me as your own, and look after me. Notice what isn't there: no list of demands, no bargaining, no I'll do this if you do that. Just a hand, a heart, feet, and belonging. And notice who is praying: a Guru who led his people through years of war. Sikhs don't hear Chaupai as a frightened prayer. They hear the request of someone who knew that being brave is not the same as being alone.

371.title: Protect me with your hand
371.hook: hamree karo hath dai rachhaa: give me Your hand and keep me safe (Chaupai)
371.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite this opening line of Chaupai Sahib each morning and evening, and some say it on its own as a short prayer before a journey or a difficult moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benti Chaupai, and your line, shelter me. This week the drums faded, the crane was found out, the secret was love, those who loved found, the ten savaiye closed, and a quiet prayer began. Today, its first line.

In Punjabi, there's an old way of saying I'll stand by you: I've taken your arm. It's a promise, the kind you don't walk away from. It's what a family does for a newcomer, an elder for a frightened child, a friend when your life falls apart. Not a handshake. A grip. And it's the first picture in the Tenth Guru's prayer for protection, the very first thing it asks for.
screen: `I'VE TAKEN YOUR ARM.` → `NOT A HANDSHAKE. A GRIP.` → `THE PRAYER'S FIRST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: The line is hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. Hamree: mine, our. Karo: make, do. Haath dai: giving your hand. Rachhaa: protection, guarding. Protect me, giving me your hand. Rachhaa is the poem's form of raksha, protection, the word also used for protective threads and amulets. But the line asks for something else: a hand. Not an object to carry around, but the protector, reaching in. The Guru isn't asking for a charm; he's asking to be held. Sikh teaching often points away from charms like these and toward the One, directly. Why a hand? Because a hand is personal. An army can protect you. A wall can protect you. But only someone right there, close enough to touch, can give you their hand. The line asks God to be that near. And it asks it of someone who sees everything, as later lines say, so it isn't a request to be noticed. It's a request to be held, while noticed. Near its close, this same prayer returns to the picture from the hook: the one who has taken my arm. We'll get there on day three hundred seventy-eight. For now, just the first line. Hamree karo haath dai rachhaa. Keep me by the hand.
